name: Mango
perishability: Perishable once ripe (4–7 days). A strictly seasonal fruit: fresh supply runs February to August.
summary: India grows close to half the world's mangoes, across hundreds of named varieties that arrive in a fixed sequence: Alphonso and Banganapalli from the South and West first, Dasheri, Langra and Chausa from the North last. The crop is decided at flowering in December–March, when fog, rain or a warm winter can halve the harvest.
global: India is the largest producer, but exports a small share of its crop (fresh fruit mainly to the UAE, UK, USA, Qatar, Oman, Kuwait; mango pulp to the Gulf and Europe). The US accepts Indian mangoes after irradiation; Japan and Korea after vapour heat treatment.

rows.hubs: Odisha, Maharashtra (Konkan Alphonso), West Bengal (Malda), Kerala, Jharkhand

belts.name: Konkan coast
belts.note: Alphonso (Hapus), GI tagged; first arrivals in Feb–Mar at Vashi.

belts.name: Rayalaseema and Krishna
belts.note: Banganapalli (GI) and Totapuri; Chittoor is the pulping capital.

belts.name: Varanasi and Bhagalpur
belts.note: Langra (Banarasi Langda GI), Jardalu (GI), Chausa; Jun–Aug.

seasons.name: South and West early varieties
seasons.note: 'Sow' here means flowering. Alphonso, Kesar, Banganapalli, Badami.

lean_season: September–January: no fresh domestic mangoes. Pulp, frozen and imported fruit only.

climate.v: Needs a cool, dry spell (roughly 10–20 °C) in winter to flower well. Warm winters mean poor flowering.
24–30 °C during fruit growth; fruit drops in heat above ~42–45 °C.
Rain, fog or cloud at flowering (Dec–Mar) brings powdery mildew, anthracnose and hoppers; dry weather from flowering to harvest is ideal.
Many varieties (Alphonso, Dasheri, Langra) give a heavy crop one year and a light one the next.
Deep, well-drained soil, pH 5.5–7.5; altitude up to ~600 m for commercial crops.

weather_risks.risk: Fog, rain or cloud at flowering
weather_risks.impact: Flowers blacken (powdery mildew, anthracnose), hoppers multiply, and fruit set collapses.
weather_risks.example: Unseasonal winter rains cut Konkan Alphonso output in several recent seasons.

weather_risks.impact: Weak or late flowering; vegetative flush instead of flowers.
Heavy fruit drop and scarring just before harvest.
weather_risks.example: Nor'westers (kalbaisakhi) in Bengal and Bihar each spring.
Cyclone Tauktae (May 2021) hit Konkan Alphonso and Gir Kesar.

pests.name: Mango hoppers
pests.impact: Suck sap from flowers; flowers and young fruit drop.

pests.name: Powdery mildew
pests.impact: White coating on flowers; poor fruit set.

pests.name: Anthracnose
pests.impact: Blossom blight in the field and black spots on ripening fruit.

pests.name: Fruit fly
pests.impact: Maggots inside ripe fruit; the main quarantine issue for exports.

pests.name: Stone weevil
pests.impact: Quarantine pest in South India; blocks some export markets.

pests.name: Malformation
pests.impact: Bunchy, sterile flower clusters in North India.

postharvest.shelf_cold: 2–4 weeks for mature fruit at the right temperature.
postharvest.respiration: Climacteric; ripens after harvest; responds to ethylene.
postharvest.chilling: Chilling injury below ~10–12 °C: grey skin, uneven ripening, poor flavour.
practices: Harvested at physiological maturity with a short stalk, then de-sapped to avoid sap burn.
Ripened with ethylene (10–100 ppm) at 20–25 °C; calcium carbide is banned and FSSAI runs enforcement drives every season.
Export treatments: hot water (EU and others), vapour heat (Japan, Korea), irradiation (USA).
Alphonso is sold per dozen and in 4–6 dozen wooden boxes (peti); most others per kg.

steps.what: Many owners sell the standing crop at flowering to a pre-harvest contractor, who carries the weather risk.
Contractor picks, grades and packs in wooden boxes, crates or cartons.
Vashi (Navi Mumbai) for Alphonso; Lucknow, Azadpur, Kolkata for northern types; Chittoor pulp units for Totapuri.
Traders ripen in chambers or traditional straw-and-paper stacks.
Domestic retail, quick commerce, online direct-from-farm boxes, and export pack houses.

supply_chain.packaging: Wooden boxes and plastic crates (domestic); CFB cartons with grading (export).
supply_chain.farmer_share: About 43% of the retail price in the domestic chain (RBI, 2024).

markets.name: Vashi APMC
markets.role: Largest Alphonso market; season opens with ceremonial first boxes.

markets.name: Krishnagiri
markets.role: Totapuri and Neelam for pulp and table.

varieties.name: Alphonso (Hapus)
varieties.note: Konkan; Mar–May; premium, sold per dozen.

trade.exports: Fresh mango exports are a few tens of thousands of tonnes a year (UAE, UK, USA, Gulf); mango pulp exports are larger.

policy.what: USA opened to Indian mangoes with irradiation.
Calcium carbide ripening banned; ethylene permitted.
APEDA's MangoNet traceability for export orchards and pack-house approvals.

history.what: Cyclone Tauktae destroyed Konkan and Gir orchards weeks before harvest.
First Alphonso boxes at Vashi sell at ₹1,500–5,000+ per dozen; prices fall as volumes rise.
Alternate bearing plus bad flowering weather can cut regional output by half.

signals: Flowering reports (Dec–Feb) from Konkan, AP and UP horticulture departments.
Fog days and rainfall during Jan–Mar in mango districts.
First-arrival dates and daily box counts at Vashi APMC.
Heat and storm warnings in Apr–May for the North.
business: The variety calendar is the product calendar: a buyer can run five months of supply by moving from Alphonso to Kesar, Banganapalli, Dasheri, Langra and Chausa.
Pre-harvest contractors carry most of the weather risk and capture most of the margin in good years.
Residue-free, carbide-free certification and direct farm boxes command strong premiums in metros.
Pulp and frozen chunks extend the season to 12 months for food-service buyers.
